name: The City of God and the earthly city (the two cities)
plain_explanation: Augustine imagines all of history as the story of two intermingled 'cities' or communities: one belonging to God and destined for eternal reward, the other belonging to the world (and ultimately to the Devil) and destined for eternal punishment. In this life the two are mixed together and cannot be told apart with certainty; only at the end will they be separated.
precise_definition: A providential scheme of history in which the elect (predestined for salvation, symbolized by Abel) belong to the pilgrim 'City of God,' and the reprobate (symbolized by Cain) belong to the earthly city doomed to eternal torment with Satan; in this life the two cities are commingled, but they will be definitively separated at the Last Judgement.
why_it_mattered: It supplied the theoretical justification, throughout the Middle Ages, for the claim that the State should be subordinate to the Church in religious matters, since only the Church truly represents the City of God on earth.
historical_origin: Developed across The City of God (412-427) in answer to pagans who blamed the sack of Rome (410) on the abandonment of the old gods.
examples: Cain belonging to the city of the Devil, Abel to the City of God
Augustine's argument that Christians who suffered in the sack of Rome have no right to complain, since worldly loss cannot touch what truly matters
competing_positions: The pagan view that Rome prospered under Jupiter's protection and fell once the old gods were abandoned
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell traces its influence through the medieval struggles of Church and Empire, and draws his own analogy to Marx's philosophy of history (Yahweh/Dialectical Materialism, the Messiah/Marx, the elect/the Proletariat, the Church/the Communist Party, the Second Coming/the Revolution), presented explicitly as Russell's own device for explaining Marxism's emotional appeal, not as a claim Augustine himself made.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political and religious: became, in Russell's account, the doctrinal basis for the medieval claim that secular rulers must be submissive to the Church, a position realized far more fully in the weak Western Empire than in the strong Byzantine East.
